text:
How do apps handle a million tasks without threads tripping over each other? Often with a mutex. It guards a critical section, the code that touches shared data. Only one thread can hold the lock at a time, so two threads never modify that data simultaneously. Think of a bouncer at a nightclub: one guest goes in, and the rest wait their turn.

Mutexes can go wrong, though. If threads grab locks in the wrong order, you can get a deadlock, where every thread waits forever.

On Linux, mutexes are built on futexes, which skip the expensive system call whenever the lock is uncontended. In the common case, locking is fast.

Whether you're building a game or a banking app, you'll reach for mutexes again and again.
